title: What to publish before you run ads
metaTitle: What to publish before you buy ads
excerpt: Publish the offer, the proof, and a way to talk before you buy traffic. Ads pointed at a vague homepage pay for clicks a cold visitor cannot use.
alt: Smooth overlapping waves of blue, violet, and warm orange, layered color for an article about the pages that must exist before you pay for a visit.
caption: Layers of color, in place before anyone is asked to look. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Which pages should exist before you pay for traffic?
faqs.answer: Publish the offer, proof that matches that offer, and a way to start a conversation. Each proof needs a sentence about the decision, not only a picture. A manifesto, a careers page, and a large archive can wait until a cold visitor can already tell what you do.

faqs.question: Should every ad point at the homepage?
faqs.answer: Give each campaign a page that repeats its promise. A homepage can introduce the studio. A campaign about one kind of work should land on that work, with a project and a next step beside it. One generic URL for every ad forces that URL to explain everything at once.

faqs.question: What should you watch in the first week of spend?
faqs.answer: Watch whether the calls match the offer you advertised, not only the cost of the click. Check that the ad line and the first sentence describe the same job. Change the sentence before you change the bid, and avoid a redesign in the middle of the flight, because then you cannot tell which page the numbers describe.

sources.title: Influencing your title links in search results

markdown:
Content before paid ads is the set of pages a buyer needs if they arrive with no memory of you: the offer, the proof, and a way to talk. An ad can buy the click. It cannot explain a company the landing page has left unexplained.

Publish those pages before you fund the visit. A vague homepage turns paid traffic into a bill for a bounce, and it teaches the wrong lesson about the channel.

## The pages a cold arrival actually uses

Assume the person has never heard the name. They saw one line, tapped it, and opened a tab between other tasks. The page has to confirm the promise, show that the work is real, and offer a next step they can accept without scheduling a meeting about the meeting.

Three surfaces do that job.

1. The offer, in the buyer's language, with an edge around what you will not take.
2. Proof that matches the promise, each project with the decision in one sentence.
3. A way to talk, with the purpose of the conversation written beside the action.

A manifesto, a careers page, and a full archive can wait. They do not help this visit decide. [Google's helpful content guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) asks whether a page has a primary purpose a person came for, and whether someone can tell who created it. The purpose of a page you are about to advertise is the conversation that follows a clear offer. Your name should be visible without a hunt through the footer.

Write the offer the way you would say it on a call. "We design and build the marketing site, and you leave with the repository." That sentence can be advertised. A line about crafting experiences cannot, because the visitor cannot tell what they would be buying, and neither can the person who has to take the call afterward.

## Write the ad from a page that already exists

The page comes first. If a sentence is not true on the site, it is not ready to be a paid line. People who feel misled in the first screen do not become a useful story about the channel. They become a second-guess you paid to collect.

[Google's guidance on title links](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/title-link) asks for titles that describe the page clearly, and it notes that vague or boilerplate titles are the ones that get rewritten. Use the same standard across the ad, the title element, and the visible heading. They should name the same job. A difference in tone is fine. A difference in offer means you bought the wrong click, then asked the page to apologize.

Give each campaign one landing page. A homepage can introduce the studio. A campaign about moving a store should land on a page about that work. Down the Cove, an ecommerce migration and redesign, is the kind of proof that belongs under a commerce promise. A campaign about product interfaces should land beside work like Got Next, Leadly, or Trade Moai, where the screen is the evidence. Sending every ad to one generic URL forces that URL to be every page.

Check the page on a phone before you approve the spend. The heading, the proof, and the action should appear without a precise scroll. If the first view is a full-bleed image and a slogan, the ad's promise is waiting under the picture for a person who may not go looking. Pay for the view you would be willing to see yourself, on a small screen, in a hurry.

## Proof a suspicious reader can inspect

Someone who clicked an ad is already a little guarded. They have been sold to today. Proof has to be a decision they can read, not a strip of logos with no story attached.

Name the constraint in the caption. For a shop, say what moved and what the customer still recognizes. For an editorial site, say what the reading experience had to protect. Thomas Bewick is a public example of a heritage craft carried onto a modern site. Ballarat Box Sports is a public example of a community brand with a specific audience. Use the project that shares a problem with the ad. A tactile brand world such as Wabisabi is the wrong neighbor for an ad about checkout, even when the pictures are the best thing in the folder.

Leave out numbers you cannot explain on a call. A percentage with no source. A quote polished past what anyone said. A timeline that was never the plan. The click may not audit you. The founder who books time will, because the conversation will be about the work, and a fuzzy caption becomes a long correction.

Put the proof near the promise, not in a museum the visitor has to discover. One strong project next to the offer beats eight projects on a page the ad never mentions. If you only have adjacent work, say it is adjacent. Honesty about the gap is safer than a crop that implies a fit you have not earned. A reader can respect a smaller claim. They remember an inflated one.

## A next step that matches the click

The action should be as specific as the line that earned the click. If the ad offered a look at how a marketing site gets scoped, the button should offer that conversation. If the ad offered a store migration, say so on the button. A generic label after a specific promise feels like the page changed its mind on the way down.

Say what the half hour is for. Fit, the shape of the work, and whether a proposal is worth writing. Say what it will not cover. You will not redesign the site live. People who are ready use a clear door. People who are browsing leave, which is a kinder result than a form left unfinished at the ninth field.

If you use a form, keep it to what you need in order to prepare. Name, email, the current URL, and one line on the job. Ask the rest when you can hear the answer. A long form is a second product the visitor did not agree to, and the ad is not paying them to finish it. Every extra field is a place for a tired person to decide the tab can wait.

The technical facts belong in one sentence, after the offer is clear. A public site built in Next.js, React, and TypeScript, styled with Tailwind, and deployed on Vercel tells a technical buyer they will own a codebase. It is a poor headline for an ad, and a poor substitute for the proof. Mention it where the fear shows up, which is usually after they believe you can design the thing.

## What should stay offline until the offer is stable

Keep these off the paid path until they are true.

- A service line that is still a guess you have not said out loud.
- Proof that is a concept you have not shipped.
- A staging site behind a password.
- A one-page site that addresses three audiences and hopes the right one will self-select.
- A headline you would be embarrassed to repeat once the call starts.

Also finish the unglamorous pieces before you spend. The footer should carry the real name and a way back to the offer. The page should show the heading before it shows a reel. Motion, if you use it, should wait until the promise is readable, and it should respect a request for reduced motion. A loading animation is a strange thing to buy traffic for. So is a font that delays the first sentence.

Read the landing page as if you had paid for your own click. Can you say the offer in one breath. Can you point at a project. Can you see how to talk to a person. If any answer is no, the page is still a draft. A draft with a budget becomes an expensive critique. Give it the edit while the edit is free.

## How to read the first week you pay for

Judge the page by conversations that match the offer, not by the cheapest click. Write the definition of a good call before the campaign starts, while you are still calm. A low cost and no calls is a page problem or an offer problem. A higher cost and a few serious conversations can still be the right trade. Decide that in advance so a dashboard does not talk you into the wrong fix.

In the first days, check three things.

1. The ad line and the first sentence on the page describe the same job.
2. People who stay can reach the action without hunting past the proof.
3. The calls are about the offer you paid to describe, or they reveal one sentence you should fix.

Change the sentence before you change the bid. A week of traffic is a critique you funded. Use it on the words. A redesign in the middle of the flight makes the numbers unreadable, because you no longer know which page earned the click. Pause, edit, then resume against the page you actually mean.

Share the landing URL with the person who will take the calls. If they have not read the page, they will describe a different offer on the phone, and the visitor will feel the seam between the ad and the voice. The page and the call are one introduction split across two rooms. They should sound like the same room.

## Preparation has a limit

A clear set of pages does not guarantee a channel. Some offers have no audience that responds to this kind of spend. Some weeks are simply the wrong weeks. A better-known name can still beat a clearer page. What the preparation prevents is paying to discover that the homepage cannot hold a stranger who arrived on purpose.

If the offer itself is fuzzy, stop spending. Write the boundary. Show one real proof. Then consider the auction. Ads are a poor workshop for discovering what you sell. They are a fair test of a sentence you are already willing to repeat to a founder who is slightly skeptical.

When the pages you need are really for investors, the skim changes. They look for what the company is, why it exists now, and whether the team can ship. That standard is the subject of [a website for a seed round](/blog/a-website-for-a-seed-round). Read it before you point a fundraise note at a homepage built for customers.

If you want a public list that already names the work, the boundary, and the path into a conversation, review [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). Bring your current page to the comparison. The gap you can point at is the brief, and it is cheaper to see it before the first invoice from the ad platform.
